text:
GILFILLAN ESTATE -- U.S. Senate candidates agreed with each other at times, but often disagreed at Farmfest Wednesday.

Democrat Angie Craig talked about her view of the federal government.

"The across the board, tariffs the president and administration put in place and the war in Iran that has driven up many costs for so many people in the country and can't get year around E15 (gasoline) across the finish line," she said. "If this administration's policies aren't corrected, we're going to have lots of difficulty in farm country."

Democrat Peggy Flanagan said she's heard frustration about many obstacles including tariffs and an illegal war with Iraq."

"Farmers deserve a farm bill that puts them first," she said.

Republican Michele Tafoya said she and her husband love Minnesota so they settled here.

"I see Minnesota in a little bit of pain now. We all need agriculture," she said. "We need a farm bill and trade deals to help everyone do better. California wants to tell the rest of the country how to produce pork with Proposition 12. It puts up barriers. We need nationwide regulations on how to do it," Tafoya said.

Royce White described his viewpoint.

"We've had a complete departure of common sense in the U.S. Senate," he said. "The protected elites call the this time a managed decline, but they managed it. We need to get rid of theater on how to produce pork."

White got a positive response from many people when he stood up and asked everyone who "stands up for the sanctity of life to stand up."

Craig accused Republicans of cutting billions of dollars out the farm bill that created unfunded mandates for counties.

"You'll understand when you see your next county property tax bill. Republicans cut $187 million from SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, formerly known as food stamps)," she said. "The federal government created unfunded mandates we can't afford."

Flanagan said the SNAP cuts were cost shifts creating tax cuts for the ultra wealthy.

"SNAP put food on my family's table when I was young," she said. "I'm eager to serve on the agriculture committee."

Craig admitted some tariffs are appropriate but the federal government declining to renew USMCA (U.S.-Mexico-Canada) trade deals was a mistake.

"Forty percent of U.S. farm workers are undocumented. If they obey laws, they should have a path to citizenship," she said, drawing applause.

Tafoya said it's time to help farmers pass on the farm to future generations.

"It's time to get rid of the death tax," she said.

"Farmers need workers and we need secure borders," said Tafoya. "It's not against the law to take advantage of U.S. citizenship. We need to allow farmers to innovate. We all need biofuel, renewable fuels and sustainable aviation fuel."

White said legal immigrants need a pathway to amnesty, but illegal immigrants should be mass deported to secure our borders.

He called for getting rid of excessive government regulations.

Craig said E15 passage hasn't happened because the Trump administration is in the back pocket of big oil.

Tafoya called for public-private partnerships for make it easier for people to prosper.

Craig said technology companies should pay for all added costs created by new data centers.

She called for the return of animal health programs that were cut by Republicans in Washington.

"Midwest farm bankruptcies are up 70%. This is golden age of agriculture. We all know that," said Craig. "You didn't vote for illegal tariffs and a war in Iran. We're in a spiral of ad hoc agriculture assistance. What we need is good farm policies. I'll definitely serve on the Senate Agriculture Committee."

"Diseases are coming back after prevention programs were cut," said Flanagan.

The primary election is Tuesday, Aug. 11.

Farmfest concludes at 3 p.m. today. The Women in Agriculture Event and Female Farmer of the Year Award program begins at 10:45 a.m. in the Forum building.

title: Hydrogen Powered Aircraft: The Future of Sustainable Aviation - Sustainiam
description:
While Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is helping reduce emissions from today's fleets, hydrogen powered aircraft are emerging as one of the most promising long-term solutions for sustainable aviation.
Hydrogen vs Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Hydrogen and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) are often discussed together, but they solve different challenges.
Challenges Holding Hydrogen Aviation Back Despite its promise, hydrogen aviation still faces several technical and commercial hurdles.
The Future of Hydrogen Powered Aircraft Hydrogen is unlikely to replace conventional aviation fuel overnight.
Conclusion Hydrogen powered aircraft represent one of the most exciting developments in the journey toward sustainable aviation.
text:
While Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is helping reduce emissions from today's fleets, hydrogen powered aircraft are emerging as one of the most promising long-term solutions for sustainable aviation.

Powered by clean hydrogen, these next-generation aircraft have the potential to significantly reduce aviation emissions while reshaping how the industry approaches air travel. Although the technology is still evolving, growing investments from aircraft manufacturers, governments, and energy companies are accelerating its development.

In this blog, we'll explore how hydrogen powered aircraft work, the latest industry developments, the challenges that remain, and what their rise means for the future of sustainable aviation.

Why Sustainable Aviation Matters More Than Ever?

The demand for air travel continues to grow despite increasing pressure to reduce emissions.

Passenger traffic is expected to continue expanding over the coming decades. More flights, however, also mean greater fuel consumption and higher greenhouse gas emissions if cleaner alternatives are not adopted.

Traditional jet fuel has powered aviation for decades because of its high energy density and reliability. Yet it remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels, making it one of the most difficult sectors to decarbonize.

Unlike industries that can transition relatively quickly to renewable electricity, aviation faces unique challenges:

Aircraft require extremely energy-dense fuels.

Long-haul flights demand lightweight, high-performance energy sources.

Safety and certification standards are among the most rigorous of any industry.

Existing airport infrastructure has been built around conventional aviation fuel.

These challenges have encouraged the industry to pursue multiple pathways toward airline sustainability, including:

Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF)

Hydrogen-powered aircraft

Battery-electric aircraft for short-distance routes

More fuel-efficient aircraft designs

Operational improvements such as optimized flight routes and ground operations

Rather than competing with each other, these technologies are expected to work together to reduce aviation's environmental impact over the coming decades.

Did You Know?

The aviation industry accounts for approximately 13.9% of global transport-related CO₂ emissions, making it one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize and a key focus area for climate innovation.

What Are Hydrogen Powered Aircraft?

Hydrogen powered aircraft use hydrogen as their primary energy source instead of conventional aviation fuel.

Unlike traditional aircraft that burn kerosene-based jet fuel, hydrogen-powered aircraft can generate propulsion through two primary approaches:

1. Hydrogen Fuel Cells

Fuel cells convert hydrogen into electricity through an electrochemical process rather than combustion.

The electricity generated powers electric motors, while the only direct by-products are water vapor and heat. This makes fuel-cell aircraft one of the cleanest propulsion technologies currently being developed for aviation.

Fuel-cell systems are particularly promising for regional and short-haul aircraft, where lower power requirements make them commercially viable in the near future.

2. Hydrogen Combustion

Hydrogen can also be burned directly inside specially designed gas turbines.

This approach allows aircraft manufacturers to build upon existing turbine technology while replacing fossil-based jet fuel with hydrogen. Although hydrogen combustion eliminates carbon dioxide emissions during flight, it can still produce nitrogen oxides (NOx), meaning further engineering improvements are needed to minimize overall climate impacts.

Today, manufacturers are actively exploring both technologies to determine which is best suited for different aircraft categories.

Why Hydrogen Is Different From Conventional Jet Fuel?

Hydrogen offers several advantages that make it an attractive option for the future of sustainable aircraft.

The biggest advantage of hydrogen lies in its ability to significantly reduce lifecycle emissions when produced through renewable-powered electrolysis. This aligns closely with global efforts to build sustainable aviation futures that rely less on fossil fuels and more on clean energy.

However, hydrogen is not a drop-in replacement for jet fuel. It requires new aircraft designs, cryogenic storage systems, airport refueling infrastructure, and large-scale green hydrogen production, all of which are still evolving.

This is why most industry experts now see hydrogen as a long-term solution that will complement, rather than replace, other decarbonization pathways such as Sustainable Aviation Fuel.

Hydrogen vs Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF)

Hydrogen and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) are often discussed together, but they solve different challenges.

SAF is designed to reduce emissions from today's aircraft by replacing a portion of conventional jet fuel without requiring major changes to existing engines or airport infrastructure. Hydrogen, on the other hand, requires entirely new aircraft designs but offers greater long-term decarbonization potential.

Rather than competing, SAF and hydrogen are expected to complement each other. While SAF can help reduce emissions immediately, hydrogen represents the next generation of sustainable aircraft for the decades ahead.

Latest Industry Developments

Hydrogen aviation has made significant progress over the past few years, although commercial deployment remains a long-term goal.

Airbus continues to invest in its ZEROe programme , focusing on hydrogen fuel-cell technology for future commercial aircraft. While the company has revised its original timeline to allow more time for technology and infrastructure development, it remains committed to hydrogen as a cornerstone of aviation's long-term decarbonization strategy.

At the same time, companies such as ZeroAvia are successfully testing hydrogen-electric propulsion systems for regional aircraft, demonstrating that hydrogen-powered flight is moving beyond concept designs and into real-world testing.

Engine manufacturers are also accelerating innovation. Airbus and MTU Aero Engines have expanded their collaboration to develop fuel-cell propulsion systems, while several airports across Europe are investing in hydrogen storage and refuelling infrastructure to prepare for future aircraft operations.

Challenges Holding Hydrogen Aviation Back

Despite its promise, hydrogen aviation still faces several technical and commercial hurdles.

Green Hydrogen Availability

Hydrogen is only as sustainable as the way it is produced. Today, much of the world's hydrogen still comes from fossil fuels. Expanding the production of green hydrogen, produced using renewable electricity, is essential for achieving meaningful emissions reductions.

Storage and Infrastructure

Hydrogen has a lower volumetric energy density than conventional jet fuel and must be stored either under high pressure or as a cryogenic liquid at extremely low temperatures. This requires redesigned aircraft, specialized airport infrastructure, and new refuelling systems.

Cost and Scalability

Developing hydrogen aircraft, producing green hydrogen at scale, and upgrading airport infrastructure will require substantial investment. As technologies mature and production scales, costs are expected to decline, but affordability remains a challenge today.

Safety and Certification

Commercial aviation operates under some of the world's strictest safety standards. Hydrogen aircraft must undergo extensive testing and certification before they can enter commercial service, making regulatory approval a critical part of the journey.

What This Means for Businesses?

While hydrogen-powered commercial aircraft are still years away, businesses don't need to wait to begin reducing aviation-related emissions.

Organizations can start by understanding the environmental impact of business travel and logistics through accurate carbon accounting. Measuring emissions provides the foundation for evaluating future decarbonization pathways, whether through operational improvements, Sustainable Aviation Fuel, or hydrogen-powered travel as it becomes commercially available.

This is where solutions like Sustainiam's Emissions Calculator (ECal) can help. By enabling organizations to calculate Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 emissions with audit-ready reporting, ECal helps businesses make informed decisions and prepare for evolving sustainability regulations.

Even as cleaner aviation technologies emerge, some emissions will remain unavoidable in the near term. Organizations can address these residual emissions by procuring high-integrity carbon credits through platforms like EmX , supporting credible climate action while pursuing long-term emission reductions.

The Future of Hydrogen Powered Aircraft

Hydrogen is unlikely to replace conventional aviation fuel overnight. Instead, it will become part of a broader transition that includes Sustainable Aviation Fuel, more efficient aircraft, operational improvements, and renewable energy.

As governments, airlines, energy companies, and aircraft manufacturers continue investing in hydrogen technologies, the foundations for cleaner air travel are steadily taking shape. Success will depend not only on innovation in aircraft design but also on expanding green hydrogen production, building airport infrastructure, and creating supportive policy frameworks.

For businesses, the message is clear: Preparing today through better emissions measurement, smarter procurement decisions, and credible decarbonization strategies will position organizations to benefit from tomorrow's low-carbon aviation ecosystem.

Conclusion

Hydrogen powered aircraft represent one of the most exciting developments in the journey toward sustainable aviation. While challenges around infrastructure, cost, and hydrogen production remain, continued investment and technological progress are bringing the industry closer to a future where cleaner air travel becomes a reality.

The transition will not rely on a single solution. Hydrogen, Sustainable Aviation Fuel, electric propulsion, and operational efficiency will all play important roles in reducing aviation's environmental impact. Organizations that begin measuring, managing, and reducing their emissions today will be better prepared for the next generation of sustainable aviation.

text:
Geopolitical conflicts, market pressure to decarbonize, and falling costs for new technologies have accelerated the use of green fuels in road, maritime, and air transport. In road transportation, alternatives such as natural gas, biodiesel, and electrification are becoming increasingly attractive economically. In aviation, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is the industry’s bet for the future, and its use will become mandatory in Brazil next year. Meanwhile, even stricter global rules to reduce shipping emissions are under discussion.

For each of the three modes, Valor spoke with companies and analysts about the potential and challenges of replacing fossil fuels, which will be examined in a series of articles. Whether transportation is by land, air, or sea, experts note that the issue is increasingly moving beyond sustainability teams and becoming part of business strategies to reassess costs, mitigate risks, and meet regulatory and customer requirements.

In ground transportation, the focus of the first article in the series, freight carriers remain far from being able to replace diesel as their primary fuel. However, alternatives such as electric vehicles and natural-gas truck corridors are being adopted to reduce costs. Passenger transportation companies, meanwhile, have been using biofuels since mid-2005, and the model is expected to gain momentum under Brazil’s tax reform, which will reward emissions-reduction initiatives with tax credits.

JSL, Brazil’s largest freight carrier, has been using electric vehicles in major urban centers and testing trucks powered by compressed natural gas (CNG) and biomethane on specific longer routes, particularly the corridor between inland São Paulo and the Santos coastal region, according to Guilherme Sampaio, president of the logistics company. The fuel is already being used in automotive industry projects, and some trials are underway in pulp transportation, he adds.

“Several factors are driving these initiatives. The first is fluctuations in diesel prices. We are in a six-month period when this has become very clear. The second is biomethane production capacity, which did not previously exist in Brazil. The sugarcane industry is investing heavily. In addition, infrastructure is being built with incentives from the São Paulo state government and private investment in fueling facilities,” Sampaio says.

Another relevant factor is technological progress, which has brought the performance of natural-gas trucks close to that of diesel vehicles, Sampaio notes. Acquisition costs have also become competitive. “The only difference is that the resale market for diesel trucks is much larger than for natural-gas or electric trucks. Depreciation costs are therefore higher, and that needs to be factored into the price.”

Operating costs are 10% to 20% lower when a vehicle runs on CNG. The savings are greater with biomethane when it is produced in-house. At JSL, discussions center on landfill logistics, with the biomethane produced at the sites used to fuel the trucks.

Freight carrier Jomed, which plans to expand its natural-gas fleet, has invested not only in vehicles but also in biomethane fueling infrastructure. By the end of this year, the company plans to offer a “green route” between São Paulo and Espírito Santo, with trucks fueled entirely by biomethane from landfills. The station in São Paulo is already operating, while another is expected to open in Cariacica, Espírito Santo, in the coming months.

Of the company’s current fleet of 500 vehicles, 40 run on natural gas. Two more trucks already on order will arrive in the second half of the year, and another batch is expected to be purchased by early 2027, according to Jomed Manager Carlos Ferreira. “The goal is to have at least 150 by 2030.”

“The war has signaled that this is the time to accelerate the energy transition by replacing diesel-powered trucks. The situation is forcing us to speed up a transition that had previously been expected to take place over three years.”

In addition to soaring oil prices, Ferreira cites customer demand as an incentive for the shift, as clients seek to incorporate emissions-reduction indicators into their own decarbonization targets.

The main obstacle to expanding the model to other routes across Brazil is the availability of biomethane fueling infrastructure, he says. “In major urban centers, biomethane can be added to the natural-gas network. Outside those centers, however, I can transport it only by tanker truck, and depending on the distance, the cost becomes prohibitive.”

The company expects its initial investment in new vehicles and fueling stations to pay for itself within four years through lower operating costs.

Electric vehicles have also proved economically advantageous, but only on shorter routes and when kept in nearly continuous use, according to Maria Fernanda Hijjar, managing partner at consulting firm Ilos. “Electric trucks are viable over distances of 200 to 300 kilometers and in continuous operations along established circuits. In those cases, electric trucks significantly reduce costs compared with diesel vehicles,” she says.

“A few years ago, electric vehicles were almost entirely a marketing exercise. Today, we are seeing companies actually reduce costs and use them regardless of the emissions benefits—although emissions have obviously improved as well. Companies are now making the switch because they see opportunities to reduce costs, improve efficiency, and lower the risk of fuel shortages,” Hijjar adds.

In intercity bus transportation, biofuel use gained momentum with the regulations of the Vehicle Air Pollution Control Program (Proconve), whose eighth phase for buses took effect in 2022.

According to Leticia Pineschi, managing director of the Brazilian Association of Interstate Bus Operators (Abrati), the industry is monitoring new alternatives in addition to its ongoing emissions-reduction efforts. Green hydrogen is the leading prospect for the future, but fueling infrastructure remains the biggest obstacle, particularly for medium- and long-distance routes. The same challenge also affects electrification.

In 2025, the maximum biodiesel blend was raised to 15%, and studies are underway to increase the limit and develop vehicles capable of running on 100% biofuel.

Among the companies making progress in this area is Águia Branca. According to Renan Chieppe, vice president of its passenger transportation division, 21% of its fleet already uses Euro 6 technology under Proconve P8, reducing nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions by up to 80% and particulate matter emissions by 50% compared with Euro 5. The entire fleet also runs on B15 diesel.

Pineschi says Brazil’s tax reform should also encourage biofuel use by granting credits to companies that reduce emissions. The industry still faces difficulties in measuring the fleet’s use of these fuels, she notes, prompting Abrati members to prepare social reports to track the indicators.

“Remaining dependent on fossil fuels is not viable over the medium term. The regions that supply the world are engulfed in conflict. The more we reduce that dependence, the better. This is important not only for the environment but also financially,” Pineschi says.

title: The FE - 'Substitute USSD for Bangla QR for transaction at micro-level'
description:
Digital payments will not become mainstream simply because the infrastructure exists -- people have to find it easier than the alternatives.
She argues that policymakers should initially avoid imposing burdens that discourage small merchants from adopting digital payments.
One merchant, one QR: The original attraction of Bangla QR, Ms. Azam said, was its ability to replace a proliferation of payment codes.
Ms. Azam points to China as an example of how digital payments can become embedded in everyday economic activity.
For Ms. Azam, the success of Bangla QR should ultimately be measured by how far it penetrates beyond the formal banking and corporate sectors.
text:
The transition to cashless payments has multiple benefits for all stakeholders, especially banks and financial institutions who can avoid costs of holding and transporting physical cash, says noted financial-sector executive Ms. Humaira Azam.

Ms Azam, who has spent 36 years in Bangladesh's financial markets and is now managing director of LankaBangla Finance, argues that the country cannot build a genuinely cashless economy by designing payment systems only for smartphone users.Bangladesh market analysis

She suggests substituting universally user-friendly USSD or unstructured Supplementary Service Data for the QR (quick-response) code usable only on the smartphone.

Her question is straightforward: "How many people actually own smartphones?"

She advocates for using the USSD system, instead. "If we use the USSD system, then it can be popularised for everyone."

The proposition is particularly relevant as Bangladesh seeks to expand Bangla QR beyond banks and established merchants to millions of small businesses, including tea stalls and street vendors.

The Bangladesh Bank has said about 2.2 million merchants have so far been converted from multiple QR codes to Bangla QR, an interoperable system designed to allow a merchant to receive payments from different banks and mobile-financial-service providers through a single code.Personal finance advice

"If you want to reach even a tea stall with this QR code, you need a regimented team as well," she says, sitting at her office on Kemal Ataturk Avenue in Dhaka's Banani commercial district. "A structured team needs to visit them, set up these QR codes on-site, and teach them how to use them."

The challenge, she says, is not simply technological. It is about onboarding, usability and incentives.

"Challenges are certainly there," Ms. Azam says. "But as I said -- all these businesses across platforms -- these 12 million enterprises, which might even grow as more people enter this business network -- how will you onboard everyone?"

Ms. Azam believes Bangladesh should learn from countries that have already moved towards large-scale digital payments, while adapting those models to local conditions.

She points to India's Unified Payments Interface, or UPI, as an example of how a digital- payment system can be formalised and made accessible on a mass scale.

For Bangladesh, however, the first priority should be simplicity.

"If we use the USSD system, then it can be popularised for everyone," she said.

There should be no unnecessary delays or obstacles. Digital payments will not become mainstream simply because the infrastructure exists -- people have to find it easier than the alternatives.

That brings the discussion back to cash.

She argues that policymakers should initially avoid imposing burdens that discourage small merchants from adopting digital payments.

"You should remove those taxes for now, make it simple and user-friendly, and onboard them first," she says. "Then observe what kind of revenue the business generates, and based on that, decide what rate of tax to apply and how to collect it."

One merchant, one QR: The original attraction of Bangla QR, Ms. Azam said, was its ability to replace a proliferation of payment codes.

Previously, a merchant might need separate QR codes for different banks and mobile-financial- service providers. The "One Merchant, One QR" concept is intended to remove that complexity.

Previously, a merchant had to use separate QR codes for different banks and MFS providers. "Now, by using Bangla QR, what we actually want is to build a cashless society."

A single interoperable QR code can reduce the friction involved in accepting digital payments while potentially lowering the costs associated with handling and securing physical cash.

But Ms. Azam cautions that Bangladesh is still at the beginning of the journey and needs a lot of steps. Those steps will inevitably involve trial and error.Bangladesh market analysis

"Many steps will be required to smooth this out," she said. "We need to do more trial and error. Because we already know that its usage has started, it takes some time for people to learn it and to get used to it."

Ms. Azam points to China as an example of how digital payments can become embedded in everyday economic activity.

"In a country like China, from utility bill payments to small purchases, they use WeChat and QR codes everywhere -- for every little transaction -- and it is working just fine."

Bangladesh does not have to invent the model from scratch. "You are adopting a proven concept. So it's very easy to use this system. Even if flaws exist, you can look at how other countries eliminated their flaws and resolve yours using their examples."

She has highlighted central bank's cost to replace the torn notes.

The central bank also bears costs associated with producing and replacing notes, while commercial banks have to insure, transport and store physical currency.

"Think about the millions of damaged banknotes and their re-printing costs. It's a real cost to the country," she says.

Her conclusion is blunt: the economy should move towards a system in which transactions are increasingly settled digitally rather than through physical currency.

"We need to get rid of all this. It has to transition to a system-based environment where no actual physical cash is exchanged; it's just a smooth transaction being completed. That is where we need to arrive."

For Ms. Azam, the success of Bangla QR should ultimately be measured by how far it penetrates beyond the formal banking and corporate sectors.

Educational institutions should accept it for fees. Hospitals and clinics should be able to use it around the clock. Government service counters should accept digital payments. Rural and semi-urban merchants should be included.

And, eventually, even the smallest businesses should have access.

That will require a sustained effort over the next five years, she argues-not merely a policy announcement.

The authorities will need to systematically popularise the system, ensure merchants receive QR codes, deploy teams to install them and educate both merchants and customers about how to use them.

One argument against moving too quickly towards a cashless economy is the loss of seigniorage -- the benefit a central bank derives from issuing currency. Ms. Azam believes focusing only on this source of income misses the broader economics of cash.

"You are looking at only one side of it," she says. "But have you ever thought about the total operational costs related to cash?"

Banks and financial institutions incur significant costs in holding physical currency. "Firstly, they pay massive insurance premiums due to vault-limit restrictions. Secondly, that money sits idle as an unproductive asset, not contributing to the velocity of GDP. It just sits there unused."

Then come the costs of replacing worn banknotes, transporting cash and maintaining security.

"Furthermore, consider the additional reprinting costs for replacing worn-out bills. When you factor in all these -- human effort, transport, security costs, armoured vehicles -- these expenses add up significantly."

A reduction in physical cash, she argues, would eliminate or reduce many of these costs.

"All these costs get eliminated. The less idle, unusable cash we have, the better it is for the economy."

For Ms. Azam, therefore, the debate over cash versus digital payments should not be reduced to the revenue generated from issuing banknotes. It should be treated as a broader cost-benefit question for the economy.

"A cashless society is very important," she says. "Why do you think Western nations and major global economies are reaping the benefits right now?"

Par Pacific Holdings Inc. released second quarter financial results on Aug. 5, reporting its Hawaii renewable fuels facility ramped up production during the three-month period after commencing operations in April.

The biorefinery, located at the company’s Kapolei refinery, has the capacity to produce 61 MMgy of renewable diesel, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), renewable naphtha and low-carbon liquefied petroleum gases. The project is designed to have the flexibility to produce up to 90% SAF or 90% renewable diesel.

The Kapolei refinery originally had the capacity to produce approximately 94,000 barrels per day of conventional fuels. Par Pacific in April 2023 announced plans to make an estimated $90 million investment to convert one of the refinery’s production units to renewables. The biorefinery began operations in April 2026.

Par Pacific Holdings Inc., Mitsubishi Corp. and ENEOS Corp. on in July 2025 announced plans to establish Hawaii Renewables LLC, a joint venture to produce renewable fuels at the Kapolei refinery. The joint venture closed in October 2025. Mitsubishi Corp. and ENEOS Corp., through Alohi Renewable Energy LLC, acquired a 36.5% equity stake in Hawaii Renewables in exchange for cash consideration of $100 million. Under the agreement, Par Pacific retained the remaining interest and will and operate the renewable fuels facility through its affiliate, Par Hawaii Refining LLC.

During a second quarter earnings call, Par Pacific President and CEO Will Monteleone confirmed the company’s Hawaii renewable fuels business made steady progress during the quarter. “Renewable diesel production ramped through the quarter with June throughput reaching approximately 3,000 barrels per day before we commenced the Hawaii plant-wide turnaround,” he said. “In addition, we completed first commercial renewable diesel sales during the quarter. Volumes were small and reflect the early-stage nature of the commercial ramp, but they established the operational pathway from production to sales.”

Richard Cramer, executive vice president of refining and logistics at Par Pacific, said the company currently expects renewable throughout to average between 1,500 and 2,000 barrels per day during the third quarter, reflecting the plant turnaround even in July through early August.

text:
MORGAN, Minn. — While U.S. Rep. Brad Finstad spent Tuesday afternoon at Farmfest saying the House has done its job on the farm bill and the Senate needs to finish it, his DFL challenger said the bill has been stuck for eight years and that the incumbent owns part of that.

Finstad, R-New Ulm, and Jake Johnson, a math teacher at Rochester Mayo High School, appeared at the 1st and 2nd District candidate forum in the Wick Buildings Farmfest Center at the Gilfillan Estate, one week before Minnesota's Aug. 11 primary. Both spoke separately with Agweek afterward.

Political forums are a hallmark of Minnesota Farmfest. Appearing onstage with Finstad and Johnson were candidates for Minnesota's 2nd Congressional District: DFL candidates Kaela Berg, Matt Klein and Matt Little and GOP candidate Eric Pratt.

Finstad, a fourth-generation farmer serving on the House Agriculture Committee, pointed to the Farm, Food and National Security Act of 2026, which the House passed 224-200 on April 30. It was the first farm bill to clear the chamber since the 2018 law, which has run on extensions since 2023 and expires again Sept. 30.

"We need them to show us, the American public, that they're willing to get a farm bill on the desk of the Senate that they can pass and get us to the negotiating table with a conference committee," Finstad said.

The Senate Agriculture Committee is scheduled to mark up its own version, Chairman John Boozman's Agricultural Act of 2026, on Thursday. Senators leave for August recess the following day. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., is the committee's ranking member, and Finstad said he hopes she uses the post to move the bill.

Johnson said farmers have heard timelines before.

"It's one thing to say we need to deliver. It's another thing to deliver," Johnson said, listing year-round E15, sustainable aviation fuel and a fix for California's Proposition 12 as items that keep stalling. "There has not been a farm bill delivered since he's been in Congress. That's just a fact."

An amendment to allow year-round E15 sales was stripped from the House bill before passage and handled separately. Boozman's Senate text includes permanent year-round E15.

Johnson said the House bill leaves the two biggest problems untouched — input costs and export markets he said tariffs have gutted.

The seat the two are vying for is one that Finstad won in an August 2022 special election following the death of Rep. Jim Hagedorn. He was reelected in 2024 with 58.6% of the vote. The district, which stretches along the Iowa border and is anchored by Rochester, backed President Donald Trump by about double-digit percentage points in 2024 and 2020.

It's a seat that's swung before, and according to the description by the Cook Political Report, "became more competitive during the aughts, paving the way for Tim Walz, a high school teacher regarded as a longshot candidate, to flip this seat in 2006."

A February poll in Minnesota’s 1st Congressional District by Public Policy Polling, a Democratic-aligned firm, had Johnson within three points of Finstad, with 15% of voters still undecided.

Finstad has backed bridge payments to farmers, and when asked whether annual ad hoc aid is becoming a permanent feature of farm policy, he said he hopes not.

"Because that means times have not improved," Finstad said. "The needs of the farmers and the wants of the farmers is a market, not a bridge payment. We want 14, 15 dollar beans. We want $6 corn."

He credited the Trump administration with "20 new ag trade agreements" and pointed to soybeans trading about $1.50 a bushel higher year-over-year, renewable volume obligations pulling crush demand and House movement on E15. Still, he said, "right now there is a need for a bridge payment."

From the forum stage, Finstad measured the squeeze against his family's own books.

"My grandfather sold his soybeans in 1973 for $12.80 a bushel. We are not at $12.80 a bushel right now," he said, adding that inputs up more than 30% have eaten the price gains.

Rising Minnesota farm bankruptcies "should concern all of us," Finstad said, though he argued the causes stretch back to the Biden administration which left farmers "land rich and cash poor."

Johnson, who has built part of his campaign on how little of the consumer dollar goes back to the farmer, wants antitrust law already on the books enforced.

"Many of the agencies that are supposed to enforce this have been defunded through DOGE, and so there's no one left to enforce this legislation," Johnson said of the federal initiative launched by the second Trump administration that was lauded several times earlier in the day by U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins. "When we bring competition to the marketplace, that will drive down costs."

He also pointed to the issue of consolidation among U.S. farm operations, which led to the loss of more than 15,000 farms in 2025, marking seven straight years of continued consolidation of the industry, according to USDA data released in February.

Finstad rejected the framing of farm consolidation being a root to the problem for farmers' overall profits.

"Farms come in all different shapes and sizes, and I don't think it is a dipstick politician's role to say farms should be this size," he said. "I want opportunities for farmers, young and old, big and small."

For the corporate industry, Finstad said that consolidation may warrant questions, noting a bill he co-authored requiring transparency in the fertilizer market.

Finstad and Johnson agreed on one thing at the forum, with Johnson saying he was "encouraged" by Finstad's bill extending H-2A visas to year-round livestock and dairy labor, though he said the fix belongs inside broader immigration reform.

Finstad noted the program has been called temporary for 42 years.

"The time for us addressing this temporary, archaic system is now," he said.

text:
OMAHA, Neb – Six finalists have been selected to pitch at the inaugural “Biomanufacturing Shark Tank,” taking place on Day Two of Bio Innovations North America 2026. The event runs at 9:25 a.m. on Wednesday, 10 September, at the CHI Health Center in Omaha.

The finalists were chosen with help from investor partners at the NSF RuralSTAMINA Biomanufacturing Engine in Iowa and Nebraska. ADM has signed on as a financial supporter of the event.

The six start-ups pitching are:

Craft BioSolutions (Highland Park, Ill.) is building modular biomanufacturing infrastructure aimed at the “missing middle,” helping bio-based processes bridge the gap between lab-scale development and commercial production.

Ecovaleric (Boulder, Colo.) is an electrochemical manufacturing company scaling production of biomass-derived chemicals and materials. Its lead product, gamma-valerolactone, is a bio-based solvent designed to replace hazardous solvents such as NMP, DMF, and DMAc across advanced manufacturing.

Kemvera (formerly New Iridium) is a sustainable chemical innovation company converting surplus Midwest corn ethanol into low-carbon, drop-in chemicals. Its flagship products, bio-acetic acid and bio-ethyl acetate, are USDA BioPreferred-certified and target the acetyl value chain used in footwear, paints, disinfectants, and perfumes.

Låkril Technologies (Chicago, Ill.) commercializes bio-based acrylic acid using catalyst technology spun out of the University of Minnesota. The company says its process delivers cost parity with petroleum-based acrylics while cutting CO2 emissions by more than 80%.

Oleo (Berkeley, Calif.) transforms underutilized biomass waste into feedstocks for advanced fuels, including cellulosic sugars and renewable oils for ethanol, renewable diesel, and sustainable aviation fuel production.

Sustainable Chemicals develops bioplastics designed to match the cost and performance of petrochemical plastics. The company says its process cuts carbon footprint by 45% compared with petrochemical plastics and does not rely on fermentation to scale.

Each finalist will get three minutes to pitch, followed by two minutes of questions from a panel of investors and industry funders, dubbed the “Sharks.” The panel includes Lisa Dufresne, Investment Manager, Corporate Venture Capital, GC Ventures; Keith Marcinowski, Principal Scientist, Advanced Science & Technology Scouting, The J.M. Smucker Company; Chris Forgey, Senior Segment Director, ADM; and Michael Hershkowitz, Director, Global Sustainability and Sustainable Innovation, IFF.

Two winners will be chosen: one picked by the Sharks, one by the audience. Both will be announced at the close of the conference. The rest of the panel of Sharks will be announced soon.

About RuralSTAMINARuralSTAMINA (Ascending Rural communities through Sustainable, Transformative, Advanced Manufacturing Innovations and Alliances) is an Iowa State University-led research initiative. In July 2026 it won a National Science Foundation Regional Innovation Engines award, one of 12 selected nationwide. The award provides $15 million over two years, with up to $160 million available over 10 years for engines that meet research milestones.

RuralSTAMINA operates across Iowa and Nebraska, supporting agricultural producers and small and medium-sized manufacturers. Biomass conversion has traditionally targeted low-cost, high-volume fuels. RuralSTAMINA instead focuses on high-value specialty products, including coatings, pesticides, nutraceuticals, pharmaceuticals, biologics, and animal vaccines. More than 70 public and private partners across both states are involved, including the University of Iowa, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Southeast Community College, Des Moines Area Community College, BioConnect Iowa, the Iowa Biotechnology Association, and Invest Nebraska.

About Bio Innovations North AmericaBio Innovations North America takes place 9-10 September 2026 at the CHI Health Center in Omaha, Nebraska. Now in its third year, the event is dedicated to scaling industrial biomanufacturing across the region. It connects bio-based developers and producers with chemical manufacturers, consumer brands, investors, community enablers, and suppliers through curated panels, keynotes, and a pre-arranged 1-2-1 meetings program. The 2026 edition is expected to host more than 400 attendees and facilitate over 800 pre-arranged commercial meetings.

Bio Innovations North America is organized by World Bio Markets Ltd, publisher of World Bio Market Insights.

text:
Over sixty Boeing 787 widebodies were ordered at this year's Farnborough Airshow — a reminder of where airline capital usually goes. That same capital, by our estimate, could also fund roughly 30 sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) plants.

Nobody's actually choosing between buying jets and building fuel plants, of course.

But managing fuel-price risk isn't a new idea — Delta Air Lines made a version of this bet back in 2012, buying an oil refinery instead of just buying fuel from someone else. The exposure it was trying to escape then looks a lot like what airlines face with SAF now.

Air France-KLM already reports a distinct SAF premium cost line — the extra price of SAF over regular jet fuel — of about €250m for 2026, up from €230m in 2025, and that's before the EU's blending mandate jumps from 2% to 6% in 2030. On the open market, that premium is exposed to scarcity and rises every year.

So we built a model with our client GEVO, one of the leading Alcohol-to-Jet (AtJ) producers, to test a different option: what if airlines owned a piece of the SAF plant?

When your airline needs SAF to hit the mandates, are you better off buying it on the open market as prices rise year after year — or putting capital into the plant that makes it, and locking in your price and volume?

Try different scenarios in our interactive model here

Picture an AtJ plant: 100,000 tonnes a year of SAF, built for about €555m (a shade over two new Boeing 787-9s at an estimated ~€250m apiece).

Our model compares two paths:

Option one: keep buying SAF at market price, which climbs every year as mandates tighten.

Option two: put money into the plant and lock in a fixed offtake price now.

You can move the sliders yourself: offtake volume, the fixed premium, how much equity you take, expected return, today's spot price, how fast that spot price climbs, and how many years you're planning for.

What it comes out to

Let's look at a working example:

Owning ~20% equity stake in a SAF plant costs about €111m* up front. From there, run it out 10 years: stay on the open market instead, and you're looking at roughly €1.45bn in cumulative premium as prices climb**. Put the money in, and that same decade costs about €795m all in.

That's a €655m gap — for locking in your price, securing your volume, and owning a piece of the plant instead of renting fuel from it every year.

Worth mentioning: this only holds if SAF premiums keep rising the way the model assumes. Flatten that curve and the gap closes. Pull the assumptions toward your own view of where prices go, and see what changes.

* 20% of the baseline €555m plant capital

** This calculation is based on these figures in the interactive model: 100kt/yr offtake, equity return of 15%, a spot premium of ~€1,100/t rising 6% a year, and a fixed premium price of ~€850/t.

There's already a precedent

In 2012, Delta Air Lines bought the Trainer refinery outside Philadelphia for $150m net after state incentives, plus another $100m to retool it, mainly to lock down jet fuel for its New York hubs. Its CEO at the time said the price tag was about what one new widebody would cost — same comparison we're making above — and expected it to save the airline $300m a year.

It wasn't smooth: refining margins swing, and the early years were rough. But today, that refinery supplies roughly 75% of Delta's jet fuel needs through direct production and fuel-swap deals — one of the few structural fuel advantages any airline has built for itself. It also now makes renewable diesel and is looking at SAF next, feeding a Delta fuel hub in Minnesota. What made sense for jet fuel in 2012 is starting to make sense for SAF now.

Delta Air Lines isn't alone anymore, either. Turkish Airlines took a 40% stake in a Turkish biofuel producer earlier this year, as part of the carrier's broader SAF strategy.

Try it yourself

The model is indicative, built to provoke a conversation, not a term sheet. But the underlying question is real: as SAF mandates tighten globally, is buying aircraft the only place airline capital should go?

Play with the model here

We'd love to hear what you think once you've run a few scenarios!

Results for the second quarter and six months ended 30 June 2026

International network expansion driving attractive growth, engine outlook at an inflection point - addressing cost headwinds.

Almaty, Kazakhstan - Air Astana JSC (the "Company" and, together with its subsidiary FlyArystan, the "Group"), the leading airline group in Central Asia and the Caucasus regions by revenue and fleet size, announces its results for the second quarter and six months ended 30 June 2026.

Ibrahim Canliel, CEO of Air Astana, commented:

"The Group delivered strong top line growth in the second quarter of 2026, with revenue and other income accelerating by 18.3%. This was achieved with broadly unchanged capacity through disciplined pricing and Air Astana's dynamic allocation of capacity towards international markets resulting in an 18.5% RASK increase.

Unit cost growth continued to exceed unit revenue growth in Q2, as higher fuel prices at international stations persisted while the tenge remained strong and costs associated with the ongoing Pratt & Whitney engine issues had to be spread across a broadly unchanged capacity base. However, our visibility on P&W has improved significantly - we currently have around 60% fewer grounding than the equivalent period last year and anticipate zero groundings in summer 2027.

The operating environment in the Gulf remained volatile throughout the second quarter and continued to require close monitoring and rapid adjustments to schedules and capacity. The flexibility of our network enabled us to redeploy aircraft to satisfy strong customer demand in alternative markets and highlights the countercyclical nature of our operations within this 'New Normal'.

While responding to these operational challenges, we continued to execute our long-term network strategy by rebalancing capacity towards high growth international markets across both of our brands. China represents the largest area of our international expansion - following the launch of Shanghai in Q1, we added services to Guangzhou, Urumqi and Xi'an, almost doubling summer capacity to China year-on-year to up to 51 weekly flights which will serve nine destinations by the end of the year. We expanded connectivity to India, Europe, South East Asia, and Central Asia and the Caucasus, broadening travel options and strengthening transit flows through Almaty and Astana. Together, these developments broaden the Group's international reach and support Kazakhstan's growing role as a regional aviation hub."

Q2 Summary

Revenue growth continued, despite broadly stable capacity and traffic.

· Total revenue and other income increased 18.3% to USD 433.0 million (Q2 2025: USD 365.8 million).

· ASK decreased 0.2% to 5.56 billion (Q2 2025: 5.57 billion).

· RPK decreased 0.4% to 4.54 billion (Q2 2025: 4.56 billion).

· RASK-CASK differential positive for the quarter:

o RASK increased 18.5% to USD 7.78¢ (Q2 2025: 6.57¢).

o CASK increased 24.3% to USD 7.29¢ (Q2 2025: 5.87¢).

· EBITDAR decreased 3.7% to USD 93.6 million (Q2 2025: USD 97.1 million). EBITDAR margin 4.9pp lower to 21.6% (Q2 2025: 26.5%).

· PAT decreased to USD -0.1 million (Q2 2025: USD 18.0 million).

· Group passengers carried fell 1.7% to 2.45 million (Q2 2025: 2.49 million) with average load factor stable at 81.6% (Q2 2025: 81.9%).

H1 Summary

Strong revenue and passenger growth in H1, with profitability impacted by higher costs.

· Total revenue and other income increased 16.1% to USD 763.9 million (H1 2025: USD 658.2 million).

· ASK up 0.2% to 10.3 billion (H1 2025: 10.3 billion).

· RPK increased 1.1% to 8.5 billion (H1 2025: 8.4 billion).

· CASK growth outpaced RASK growth:

o RASK increased 15.8% to USD 7.43¢ (H1 2025: 6.41¢)

o CASK increased 22.2% to USD 7.30¢ (H1 2025: 5.97¢).

· EBITDAR decreased 9.7% to USD 141.7 million (Н1 2025: USD 157.0 million). EBITDAR margin 5.3pp lower to 18.6% (H1 2025: 23.9%).

· PAT decreased to USD -21.2 million (H1 2025: USD 10.7 million).

· Group passengers carried remained broadly stable at 4.4 million (H1 2025: 4.5 million) while the average load factor improved to 82.4% (H1 2025: 81.7%).

Outlook

Our growth environment remains strong and actions to adjust our network in light of ongoing conflicts continue to deliver attractive growth dynamics which we expect to support the structural tailwinds in the region. However, in the near-term we expect inflationary cost pressures to persist offsetting some of the revenue growth momentum. Our medium-term strategy, anchored on international expansion continues apace and supports confidence in our medium-term guidance:

· Realign capacity to protect margins and mitigate inflationary cost pressures, while retaining a load factor in the mid-to-low 80s.

· Expand total fleet to 86 aircraft by the end of 2030.

· Increase EBITDAR margin to mid-to-high 20s over the medium term with liquidity ratio above 25% and leverage below 3.0x Net Debt/EBITDAR.

Financial Summary

Financial update

The Group delivered strong revenue growth in Q2 2026, with revenue and other income increasing by 18.3% to USD 433.0 million (Q2 2025: USD 365.8 million), despite Group capacity remaining broadly unchanged, with ASK decreasing by 0.2% to 5.6 billion. Revenue growth was supported by Air Astana's planned reallocation of capacity towards higher-margin international routes. However, continued cost pressures resulted in EBITDAR declining by 3.7% to USD 93.6 million (Q2 2025: USD 97.1 million), with the EBITDAR margin decreasing by 4.9 pp to 21.6% (Q2 2025: 26.5%).

The traffic trend seen in Q1 2026 continued in Q2 with international capacity (measured by RPK) rising 5.5% while domestic decreased by 7.2%. This trend is in line with our planned shift to higher margin international routes and supports our growth aspirations.

RASK increased by 18.5% to 7.78 US cents in Q2 2026 (Q2 2025: 6.57 US cents) reinforcing the unit revenue recovery seen over the prior two quarters. The increase was primarily driven by planned reallocation of capacity, supported by growth in international traffic across both brands. FlyArystan notably contributed to the international growth with 21.4% standalone RASK growth. The increase in unit revenue was, however, insufficient to offset faster growth in unit costs. CASK increased by 24.3% to 7.29 US cents in Q2 2026 (Q2 2025: 5.87 US cents). Cost growth reflected continued pressure from fuel, including a 98% year-on-year increase in the average fuel price at international stations in Q2, as well as the impact of the 7% strengthening of the Kazakh tenge against the US dollar and higher employee, aircraft ownership and engineering and maintenance costs, including labour costs associated with the Pratt & Whitney engine issue. Consequently, CASK growth exceeded RASK growth by 5.8 percentage points in Q2, narrowing the RASK-CASK spread to 0.49 US cents in Q2.

The Group cost base is designed to support a recovery in production and ongoing operational resilience. Whilst actual capacity remained constrained in the second quarter, higher labour, ownership, maintenance and traffic-related costs were spread across a stable ASK base, translating to increased unit costs and margin pressure.

Costs associated with Pratt & Whitney engine issues have been the fundamental drag on profitability. Discussions with the manufacturer to improve both production and costs have been productive and we expect significant near-term improvements in both. Crucially, we see a higher level of capacity available to us in the summer 2026 with 60% fewer groundings than previously expected. We also now anticipate zero groundings for the FY 2027.

In the second quarter, we have also successfully concluded negotiations with both Almaty and Astana airports which has given us greater visibility around the traffic related costs at our hubs in the medium-term.

As at 30 June 2026, the Group maintained a strong liquidity position with cash and cash equivalents of USD 481.5 million (Q2 2025: USD 531.6 million) with a cash-to-sales ratio of 30.9% (Q2 2025: 38.5%) before available facilities. The leverage ratio stood at 2.1x Group Net Debt/EBITDAR compared to 1.3x in Q2 2025. These metrics remain comfortably within medium-term guidance and have moved year-on-year driven by lower operating cash generation as well as continued investment in fleet. Despite the reduction in cash, the Group retains a robust liquidity position and balance sheet flexibility.

Operational Update

The Group's in-house MRO and training capabilities continue to support operational efficiency by providing greater control over maintenance and training activities and flexibility in responding to technical and operational requirements.

Planning for additional hangar facilities is progressing as the Group continues to develop its heavy maintenance capabilities. At the Group's Flight Training Centre in Astana, the second EASA-certified A320 Full-Flight Simulator is now fully operational.

During the first half of the year, Air Astana continued to accelerate its digital transformation agenda with a strong focus on customer experience, operational excellence and technology modernisation. A key milestone was the successful launch of our AI-powered customer communication platform, with ongoing investments to further enhance its capabilities. We also delivered new digital solutions across airport operations and employee services, while continuing to expand our adoption of cloud technologies to improve agility, collaboration and scalability.

Air Astana continued to develop its direct digital channels in Q2 2026, adding new functionality across its website and mobile app to improve personalisation and booking convenience. The airline launched MyTrips, providing Nomad Club members with a single view of upcoming travel by automatically saving direct bookings and allowing other itineraries to be added manually. The Company also sent its first campaign powered by the new Customer Database Platform (CDP), a foundational step toward more advanced personalization of customer communications and the digital experience going forward. These enhancements supported continued growth in the direct digital channel, with mobile app monthly active users reaching a record 149,000 in June, up 18% year-on-year.

Finally, Air Astana uplifted close to 80% of its fuel in Kazakhstan where it sources primarily from the refineries directly and manages all the logistics including transportation. Both pricing and supply through this channel have been very stable despite the conflict in the Gulf. Our international uplift (c.20%) was 25% hedged in Q2. We have not experienced any supply issues locally or internationally during the quarter.

Traffic and network expansion

During Q2 2026, the Group's dynamic capacity allocation model allowed it to expand and rebalance its network towards international markets, supported by new routes and additional frequencies across both brands. The summer 2026 schedule comprises approximately 330 weekly international services (including 102 services to Central Asia and the Caucasus) and more than 500 weekly domestic services across Kazakhstan. This network expansion and its regularity is a key driver of increased connectivity and transit traffic potential.

China was the principal area of international expansion, with the Group operating up to 51 weekly services to seven destinations (nine by year end) and capacity increasing by 81% year-on-year in Q2. Air Astana launched services between Astana and Guangzhou, while FlyArystan added Aktau-Urumqi, Almaty-Xi'an and Almaty-Chongqing. These additions followed the launch of Air Astana's Almaty-Shanghai service in Q1, alongside increased frequencies to existing destinations in China. Air Astana also increased Almaty-Delhi services to twice daily and maintained three weekly services to Mumbai driving a 91% increase in ASK to India in Q2.

Across Europe and Turkey, Air Astana increased Almaty-London to four weekly services and operated 11 weekly flights to Frankfurt from Almaty, Astana and Uralsk. Services to Istanbul increased to 25 per week from Almaty, Astana and Atyrau, including twice-daily flights from Almaty. The summer programme also included new services to Larnaca and Dalaman and the resumption of seasonal routes to Podgorica, Batumi, Bodrum, Da Nang and Nha Trang.

FlyArystan further expanded its international network during Q2 with new services from Almaty and Astana to Gazipaşa-Alanya and from Astana and Aktau to Batumi. Air Astana's regional connectivity was also strengthened through increased frequencies in Central Asia and the Caucasus, including three daily Almaty-Tashkent services and twice-daily Almaty-Tbilisi services.

Continued development of the two complementary networks broadens point-to-point travel options while supporting transit connectivity through the Group's Almaty and Astana hubs. We saw an 82% increase in international connecting traffic in Q2, demonstrating the countercyclical nature of the airline in the 'New Normal' operating environment.

Fleet

The Group's fleet is expected to grow to 86 aircraft by 2030 (54 Air Astana brand, 32 FlyArystan brand). The fleet will comprise 83 Airbus A320 family and three Boeing 787-9. The first Boeing 787-9 is expected to be delivered later in 2026 and they will ultimately replace the existing Boeing 767 fleet.

Beyond 2030 we have a flexible orderbook comprising up to 50 additional Airbus A320 family aircraft and up to 15 additional Boeing 787-9 aircraft scheduled for delivery between 2031 and 2035. Our fleet plan is designed to support our long-term growth plan and provide the best possible flight experience for our discerning customer base.

Ongoing mitigation of Pratt & Whitney challenges and additional UERs

The majority of the Air Astana's fleet comprises Airbus A320 family aircraft powered by Pratt & Whitney PW1100G engines, which remain affected by contaminated powdered metal and LLP durability issues as announced in July 2023. This issue continues to require affected engines to be removed for accelerated inspections and shop visits, leading to increased aircraft groundings across the industry. The Group continues to manage the operational impact through its established mitigation plan to maximise fleet availability during peak operating periods.

In H1 2026, the Group secured 11 additional engines to support fleet availability and mitigate the operational impact of the Pratt & Whitney engine issue. More importantly, we are pleased to report that this year we have seen significant improvements in inductions, as well as faster turnaround times and the enhanced lifetime of new HPT blades. Following 11 inductions for the FY2025, we anticipate over three times that number in 2026 and have additional commitments for 2027 as well as requests for more. With this improvement, we are seeing the number of groundings around 60% lower than in the equivalent period last year and expect to have zero Aircraft-on-Ground (AOG) during the 2027 summer peak.

Q2 marks not only a step-change in our visibility on this protracted issue but an inflection point in the impact it has on our capacity. Consequently, we are confident that the unit cost impact will improve in the near term.

Excellence

Air Astana continues to invest in its inflight product and customer experience, supporting its premium positioning and long-term growth strategy. OTP for the quarter was +5.9pp to 87.6%. The trend has been maintained in July with a monthly OTP +9.2pp to 85.5%. Likewise, the NPS in June was up by 3pp to 53 and is trending higher in July.

This quarter, Air Astana completed a Critical Design Review with satellite connectivity provider SES, advancing the planned installation of Wi-Fi hardware across its A321LR fleet to enhance our passengers' business and leisure inflight experience.

Following its introduction for Nauryz, Air Astana extended its collaboration with Sandyq beyond the seasonal period reinforcing Air Astana's role as a global ambassador for Kazakhstan by promoting national identity and cultural heritage through onboard catering and cabin experience.

In recognition of the focus on customer experience and the hard work of our 7000 colleagues, Air Astana was awarded APEX Five-Star Major Airline status for the sixth consecutive year and was also named Best Overall Airline in Central and Southern Asia by APEX in 2025. The Group's continued focus on service excellence was recognised at the Skytrax World Airline Awards 2025. Air Astana was named "Best Airline in Central Asia & CIS" for the fourteenth consecutive year and received the "Best Staff Service in Central Asia & CIS" award for the ninth time. FlyArystan was also recognised as "Best Low-Cost Airline in Central Asia & CIS" for the third consecutive year.

ESG

At Air Astana we understand the importance of driving sustainability rather than reacting to its challenges. We continue to promote regional market developments in Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and evaluate both potential supply opportunities and strategic partnerships as the domestic SAF market evolves.

In lieu of that, we have recently signed a SAF MoU with an international fuel supplier in order to secure a stable, long-term supply of sustainable fuel and support our environmental aspirations. The SAF uplift is due to commence in Europe, and expand to cover additional Air Astana routes in Asia in due course.

Our modern fleet and anticipated aircraft deliveries also ensure that we continue to fly the most efficient engines. Combined with AI-driven analytics to precisely optimise fuel consumption we seek to minimise the environmental impact of travel for our passengers. Air Astana has become one of the first companies in Kazakhstan to receive the DHL GoGreen Plus Certificate, recognising its support for reducing our Scope 3 emissions.

About the Air Astana Group

Air Astana Group is the largest airline group in Central Asia and the Caucasus regions by revenue and fleet size. The Group operates a fleet of 63 aircraft split between Air Astana, its full-service airline that operated its inaugural flight in 2002, and FlyArystan, its low-cost airline established in 2019. The Group provides scheduled, point-to-point and transit, short-haul and long-haul air travel and cargo on domestic, regional and international routes across Central Asia, the Caucasus, the Far East, the Gulf, India and Europe. title: China's Green Jet Fuel Expansion Raises Pressure on Global Feedstock Supply
description:
Chinese state-owned energy companies are rapidly expanding sustainable aviation fuel production, in a state-backed buildout that could tighten global supplies of a key raw material heavily relied on by European airlines.
Driven by national strategic priorities, China announced 16 new sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) projects in the first half of 2026, compared with four in the rest of the world, according to BloombergNEF.
State-owned enterprises including China Petroleum and Chemical Corp., or Sinopec, and China National Petroleum Corp. accounted for nearly half of the new developments, marking a shift in a sector previously led by private refiners.
